title: Devadatta - Trouble in the First Sangha
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer tells the story of Devadatta, the Buddha's cousin, who opposes the aging Buddha, draws hundreds of disciples away, helps Prince Ajatasattu starve King Bimbisara, and makes three attempts on the Buddha's life, the last with a royal elephant that the Buddha stops with an elephant cry. Norman asks why the Buddha does not retire, then turns to Anathapindaka's death, where Shariputra guides a contemplation of "not me," and to Hoitsu Suzuki's poem about failing ears and eyes becoming more truly his own. Ajatasattu, shown mercy after losing a war, comes to the Buddha in remorse, and Devadatta, dying on a stretcher, takes refuge with the Buddha's hand on his forehead.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
You can all hear okay?
Well, I really enjoyed Tim's afternoon talk yesterday.
Very, very interesting.
All the things that he was talking about rhyme a little bit with what I want to talk about this morning.
It's a story from the life of the Buddha.
Most people, I think, don't know about this story, especially the details of it, which are quite interesting.
It's a story about how the Buddha had a lot of trouble with one of his disciples, Devadatta.
Quite a bit of trouble.
This story took place when the Buddha was 72 years old.
Starting from nothing at all, at the age of about 29, the Buddha began going forth in India and teaching.
By the time he was 72, the Buddha Sangha was really big.
It was all over India, and there were not one center but many, many different groups of monastics, each of which had its own teacher.
All of these groups looked to the Buddha for leadership and inspiration, occasionally coming together in large numbers, but most of the time in smaller bands.
I think everybody does know that the Buddha left home when he was pretty young, and there's a lot of controversy about that.
Maybe he was being irresponsible and so on, but he left home.
But I think not many people note the fact that he came back.
He actually came back after a while, and pretty much everybody in his family joined the Sangha after he came back.
His stepmother, Mahapajapati, was the first Buddhist nun.
His wife, Yasodhara, also became a nun.
His sister, Sundarinanda, became a nun.
His son, Rahula, became a monastic.
His father became a lay follower.
So the whole family actually rejoined with the Buddha in a new family relationship after the Buddha left home.
And Ananda, the Buddha's attendant for many years, was the Buddha's cousin.
Many of his cousins and close relations also joined the Sangha.
Devadatta, about whom this story is, was also the Buddha's cousin.
He was Ananda's brother.
Devadatta was one of the leaders of the Sangha.
He was independently leading different groups, but somehow he wasn't satisfied with this.
He wasn't satisfied with things the way they were in the Sangha, and he somehow felt the need to oppose the Buddha.
He thought that since the Buddha was older, and he was getting kind of soft and nice and kind, this was no good for the Sangha.
How are you going to whip people into shape if you're just nice and kind and everything?
Devadatta thought the Sangha had become a little bit lax, and it needed to be strengthened.
So he proposed some more stringent monastic rules, and the Buddha rejected those rules.
Devadatta felt this was a real mistake, and it was going to make the Sangha too soft.
And he just thought the Buddha was too old at this point.
The thing he should do was step aside and appoint him, Devadatta, to be the leader of the Sangha.
He was a pretty charismatic, strong teacher, Devadatta, so he went around saying this.
And of course, everybody got really upset about it, and they came to the Buddha and said, "You should put a stop to this.
This is terrible."
And the Buddha said, "Well, don't worry.
Everything will be fine."
You didn't do anything, old guy.
This went on for some time, and finally there was a big public assembly in which many groups had come together.

In this public assembly, Devadatta stood up and said to the Buddha, "I think you're getting just a little too old and soft, and we should have other rules, and I think you should step aside and appoint me to be the head of the Sangha."
And the Buddha said, "No, I don't think I want to step aside just now.
And even if I did, I would not appoint you, Devadatta, to be the head of the Sangha, because I think you're not quite yet mature enough for this role."
Which, of course, really pissed Devadatta off.
So he then openly broke with the Buddha and began trying to speak to the Buddha's disciples to lead the Buddha and come and join him.
And many did.
Many hundreds and hundreds of disciples did join Devadatta.
He was apparently a very strong teacher, very wise, very charismatic.
This was even more upsetting to members of the Buddha's Sangha, and they said to the Buddha, "You have to do something, you have to put a stop to this."
And the Buddha said, "No, no, it's all right.
Don't worry.
It'll all work out in the end.
Everything will be fine."
Well, in those days, spiritual teachers often had the support of rulers, princes, kings.
Nowadays, when you think about, "Let's buy a dharma hall," you get a headache immediately thinking of what it would take to raise the funds.
But in those days, there were no such headaches.
You just went, and a king came forth and said, "How about if we make a monastery for you here, and then maybe another one over there?"
"Sure, thanks."
The Buddha had a lot of different places to practice all around, and one of his great allies was King Vimbasara of Mahagadda, who had a son named Ajatasattu.
So Devadatta made a connection with Ajatasattu, and he said to Ajatasattu, "I think your father's too old.
I think he should step aside and appoint you, King."
And Ajatasattu thought, "Yes, this is a really good idea."
So one time when King Vimbasara was away somewhere, Ajatasattu said, "Okay, now I'm king.
That's the end of him."
And Vimbasara came home to find this the case.
He didn't know what to do, so he went to the Buddha and said, "What do you think I should do?"
And the Buddha said, "I think you should be kind and merciful."
So King Vimbasara said, "Well, son, probably that wasn't the best way to go about this, but since you have proclaimed yourself the king, I will step aside.
Please be my guest.
Please be the new king, and I'll do what I can to help you."

Which was really a wonderful thing for him to do, but Ajatasattu and Devadatta got to talking about this, and somehow or other, between the two of them, they worked up quite a degree of paranoia around the fact that, well, as long as your father is alive and free to move around and speak, you're never going to be safe.
So Ajatasattu in effect put his father under house arrest, so he couldn't move around and speak to other people.

But this didn't seem to be sufficient, so little by little he began feeding his father less food, basically starving him to death, to the point where the king's wife would smuggle in food when she came to visit him.
The visits were strictly controlled, and when it was discovered that she was smuggling food in, they didn't allow her to visit anymore, and King Bimbisara died, starved to death in his own kingdom.

Well, in the meantime, Devadatta was also, in a very similar way, quite paranoid and thought that as long as the Buddha was around, he was never going to really be able to be successful in his project to take over the Sangha.
So, believe it or not, he made three different attempts on the Buddha's life.
He tried to assassinate the Buddha three times.
The first time, he got a lieutenant to sneak into the Buddha's hut to stab him to death.
The Buddha was asleep, and he woke up in the middle of the night, and here's this guy in this hut, standing there like a deer in the headlights.
And the Buddha said, "What are you doing here?"
And the guy said, "Well, I came here to kill you, but somehow I couldn't do it.
I just can't move.
I can't see how this is possible."
Another time, the Buddha was sitting somewhere, minding his own business, and a giant boulder fell off of a mountain right onto him, and he was able, fortunately, to jump aside in time.
He looked up, and there was one of Devadatta's henchmen up there who had pushed the boulder down on him.
The third time was actually the most spectacular, and this one most people do know about.
Devadatta somehow commandeered from Ajatasattu's palace a very fierce royal elephant, and caused this elephant to rush toward the Buddha, to crush the Buddha.

Ananda was with the Buddha at the time, and yelled and pushed the Buddha aside, and the Buddha said, "No, no, it's okay," and he didn't get out of the way of the elephant, and the elephant came charging forward toward him.
Sometime before this there was a dispute in the Sangha.
People were complaining to one another, and there were two different groups with two different teachers arguing over whether or not somebody had broken the precepts.
It was a real mess, and the Buddha went around trying to patch things up, and he was totally unsuccessful.
Nobody would listen to him.
So he walked out of one of the meetings where he was trying to make peace, when they said, "Buddha, you shouldn't have to worry about this.
Let us take care of this."
So he walked out, and he walked out of the village, and he just kept on walking.
He just kept on walking, and he walked into the forest, and he said, "I think I'll be by myself for a while."
He didn't show up to practice period or anything.
People didn't know where he was.
He didn't tell anybody he was going, and he just practiced by himself in the woods peacefully.
Then one day he encountered an elephant who was the head of a big elephant band, and the same thing had happened to this elephant.

The elephant band were fighting with one another, and the elephant couldn't make peace, and the elephant got disgusted with the whole thing and left, and they just happened to meet each other in the forest.
This elephant taught the Buddha at that time a foolproof elephant cry.
There's a way that elephants make a sound that is a foolproof way of protection.
So now, in the present moment, we're getting back to the original story: the elephant's charging toward the Buddha, and the Buddha doesn't step aside.
He just makes this tremendous elephant cry, and the royal elephant stops on a dime and puts his head down, and the Buddha pats the elephant, and they walk away together.
That was the third assassination attempt on the Buddha.
Well, you can imagine what the Buddha-Sangha was feeling now.
"Buddha, you have to do something about this.
You've got to stop this.
Look what he's doing, this Devadatta."
The Buddha said, "No, no, don't worry.
Don't worry.
It'll be okay."
So, in thinking about this story, I'm wondering, maybe the Buddha should have retired.
Why didn't he retire?
Devadatta, I mean, Bimbisara retired.
Seventy years old, it's old enough to retire, don't you think?
After 70 years, you've done plenty.
What else can you do?
It's all going to be downhill from now on, so maybe you should retire.
It's a good idea to step aside and let younger people with more energy and vision take over, then you can rest and relax, and you don't have to think about anything.
And then I thought, gee, I'm going to be 70 pretty soon myself.
It's sounding better and better.
But then I thought, so what would I retire from?
Would I retire from being with my friends?
Would I retire from my many friendships and practicing with people, sitting with people?
Is that what I would retire from?
Well, how could you retire from that, when you're not really doing anything anyway?
And then I thought of my own teacher.
As far as I'm aware, so far, there have been no attempts on his life.
But many people have been complaining about him that he should be retiring.
He's 88 or 87, something like that, and he's still the abbot of the Berkeley Zen Center.
He still completely occupies the seat.
I think people have been complaining for maybe a decade, and I think now they're just tired of complaining.
They figure he'll probably live forever, and the Berkeley Zen Center will rot all around him, and he'll still be sitting there.
So I think there are two exceptions to the law of impermanence.
One is my teacher.
He's going to live forever.
And the other one is my mother-in-law, who I'm convinced is going to live forever.
But, regardless, by the way, in Japan it's not unusual for Zen teachers to retire.
They do retire.
And they have some little temple or something to go to and practice quietly.
And there have been some American Zen teachers now who have retired somehow.
I don't know what that means exactly, but they're officially retired.
From the evidence of this story, we can get the idea that there was something unbalanced in Devadatta.
He had something more than just a compassionate desire to serve the Sangha.
You get that feeling.
He was ambitious.
He had something to prove.
Ambition, I think, is something good.
To have ambition, to go forth and do things, is a really good idea.
We should honor ambition and venerate it.
Thank goodness for ambition.
We wouldn't have all the things that make our lives possible without people being ambitious and wanting to go forth and do things.
To be honest, when there's ambition, it's usually mixed up with some need to prove something or be someone.
To think that someone is unselfishly ambitious, a hundred percent, would be foolish.
But how much percent is the need to prove something?
Is it five percent, ten percent, twenty percent?
It seems like it was too high a percentage in the case of Devadatta.
There was something not quite right.
We don't know from the story what was unbalanced or painful in Devadatta's heart that caused him to have this tremendous need.
But there was too much suffering inside of him, too much of an inner need to be someone.
It's not unusual for spiritual teachers in their old age to be problematic.
I can tell you many stories of teachers who get a little off in their old age.
Such people can be quite rigorous and create a lot of trouble.
Sometimes the disciples of those teachers have to manage them somehow, deal with them somehow, not let them just rage on by creating trouble.
But I think they have to manage them with love and respect, gently.
When there's a breach, as there is here between Devadatta and the Buddha, and as there has been, certainly, in Japanese Zen and American Zen, it's really painful.
And everybody suffers.
And everybody is to blame in some way.
So the challenge is: can we manage difficulty with strength, but with love, so that we don't have a breach?
When there's a breach, there's pain in everybody's heart, and that pain influences the practice.
It influences the practice of everyone who comes.
So it's very, very important, I think, for there to be always every effort made to have good normal relations, even when there are real differences and real problems.
It's just like with a parent.
Parents get old, they cause a lot of problems, and we would be certainly justified to say, "Well, forget you, never mind about you anymore.
You're too much of a problem."
But we can't do that, right?
We have to continue to be grateful to our parents and loving to them, even though sometimes they can be quite hard to manage.
And I think we should be loving and grateful to anybody, really, who's reached an old age.
There's a kind of automatic honor and wisdom that comes with great age.
Even though it might go along with all kinds of dementia and trouble, I think we owe anybody who's reached a great age a deal of respect and loving-kindness.
The fact that, as a society, we don't much do that is a problem for us.
It shows a kind of lack of heart and a lack of real substance in our world.
Well, there's an ending to this story of Devadatta, but let's pause and leave you with this cliffhanger of what's going to happen next, and talk about something else from the Buddha's life.
As I say, the Buddha is now, at this point in his life, 72 years old.
When you're 72 years old, and I can tell you this from my own experience, you are going to have lost a lot of friends.
Your life is not going to be what it was when it was full of people that you knew for a long time.
Now, so many people who were formative in your life and really, really important to you will be gone.
At this point in the Buddha's life, Mahapajapati, his stepmother, had died.
His father had died.
Yasodhara, the nun that he was formerly married to, passed on.
Moggallana, one of his main disciples, was gone.
Even Rahula, his son, passed on at the age of 51 and predeceased the Buddha.
Now I want to tell you the story of Anathapindaka, who was one of the Buddha's most wonderful disciples.
He was a lay person, a very wealthy person, and one of the main places that the Buddha practiced was a place called Anathapindaka's Grove.
Anathapindaka, very early on, had offered this beautiful grove as a practice place for the Buddha.
Now Anathapindaka was coming to the end of his life, and I want to share with you, from Thich Nhat Hanh's text, his version of Anathapindaka's practice at the very end of his life.
Anathapindaka's main teacher was Shariputra.

Shariputra went to him as he was passing on and advised him to practice contemplation of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha: to put his mind on the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, to ease his physical pain, to visualize and think about the goodness of the Buddha, the goodness of the teaching, and the goodness of the community as he was suffering.
And Anathapindaka did that.
Then Shariputra said:
*Lay disciple Sudhata*, which was his other name, his nickname, shorter name, *lay disciple Sudhata, let's contemplate together.
My eyes are not me.
My eyes are not me.
My ears are not me.
My nose, my tongue, my body, and my mind are not me.*
Sudhata followed Shariputra's instruction.
And then Shariputra continued:
*What I see is not me.
What I hear is not me.
What I smell, taste, touch, and what I think, none of these are me.*
And Sudhata contemplated like this with Shariputra.
Shariputra then showed Sudhata how to contemplate on the six sense consciousnesses:
*Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, thinking are not me.* Shariputra continued, *the element earth in my body is not me.
Sudhata is not me.
The element water, fire, air, space, consciousness that animates my body, these are not me.
I am not found or restrained by these elements.
Birth and death cannot touch me.
And I smile because I have never been born and so I will never die.
Birth did not give me existence and death cannot take existence away.*
They practiced like this.
It's just a few words, but this went on for many hours, practicing these contemplations, and Sudhata really hearing these words, bringing his attention to each step and really feeling it.
Suddenly he burst into tears.
Shariputra was startled to see him crying and said, "Are you upset, Sudhata, because you can't follow this contemplation?"
Sudhata said, "I am not upset at all.
And yes, I am able to follow these contemplations without any difficulty.
And I am weeping because I am so deeply moved.
For more than 30 years I have been lucky enough to follow the Buddha in practice and follow the teachings, and I have always found them wonderful.
But never before have I heard a teaching as wonderful as this.
And that is why I am crying."
And Sudhata died later that day.
I don't know what you think of that, but it may sound a little abstract or hard to grasp, this business of not me, not me, not me.
The me part of our lives is the grasping part.
Of course we need that, we need that to get through our lives.
But I think as we age we need it a lot less, and at the last moment we don't need it anymore at all.
In fact, at that last moment, whatever little bit of grasping to me is still there really hinders our path and hinders our happiness.
Not me: all this litany of practices and contemplations really means it's okay to let go of this small supposed life and open our identity and our sense of self to something much, much bigger.
We can see that we have always been much bigger than me, and now in old age and finally in death we can really appreciate the largeness, the unlimitedness of ourselves, bigger than life and death.
When I was reading this, it reminded me of something from 2010, when some of you were there.
We were in Japan at Eiheiji Monastery, and Hoitsu Suzuki, Shunryu Suzuki's son, who's an older man and abbot of Rinso-in and also at that time one of the teachers at Eiheiji, was there.
We went to Eiheiji and we had the royal treatment.
We were like the boss of the monastery, and we had a special kind of tea and Dharma talk with Hoitsu.
On that trip, some of you who were there knew that every now and then I would sneak off in a corner and be scribbling things down in my notebook.
It became a book called *Escape This Crazy Life of Tears: Japan 2010*, which was a poetry diary of that trip.
I was writing down in poetry lines all the things that were happening, and I'm going to read you the lines that describe what Hoitsu said to us that night.
I think you'll see the relationship to what we just heard.
This is quoting from *Escape This Crazy Life of Tears*:
*Hojo-san, East, West, a person of zazen is the same.
Grandmother mind, the kind heart, is imagination.
Feeling for another, see them as yourself, takes imagination.
Imagination expands the heart.
One day woke, heard sound in both ears, sudden hearing loss.
My eyes don't work right either.
Age is slowly melting my body.
With each loss there's gain.
My ears, my eyes more mine now than ever before.
Not so sorry.
My ears, my eyes more mine now than ever before.
Not so.
When I lose my life to death, will my life be owned by me more than it ever was?*
Isn't that wonderful?
That was probably the greatest Dharma talk I ever heard.
It's so beautiful, just straight from the heart.
And this is an interesting thought: caring for another, really feeling for another, takes imagination.
Imagination expands the heart.

And the idea that my ears, now that I can't hear so well, are more mine than they were before, my eyes, now that I can't see so well, are more mine than they were before, and when I die my body may be more mine than ever before.
In this text from early Pali Buddhism, the terminology used is non-self or no self, not me, not me.
But in Zen we say the same thing in the opposite way.
Instead of saying non-self, we say true self, real self.
It's the same teaching: recognizing that the life I have always thought I had has never been my true life, my full life.
It's just been part of it.
When I recognize the empty, the signless and the wishless nature of my life, how beautiful it is and how fleeting, then I really have my life.
It's a life that's not just an idea in my mind, a little bit of grasping, a little bit of neediness, but it's without limit.
This reality of my life is actually present in every perception, in every thought, in every moment of consciousness.
It's always been so.
And here at the end of his life Anathapindaka can see this, and Hoitsu, I think, is seeing it at the end of his life.
He kind of goofed off a lot.
One time, I remember, 30 years ago, he was saying to me, "I've got to stop goofing off.
I've got to really start practicing.
It's a shame on me."
I remember him saying, "Do you know that I'm as old now as Dogen was when he died?
When am I going to get started?"
And he did get started.
He did.
So that in death we lose nothing and we can really be happy.
I really appreciate that teaching.
Back to Devadatta.
What happened to Devadatta?
Well, what happened was Ajatisattu is now king, and Devadatta's sangha is really growing and growing and growing.
Another king, the king of Kosala, Pasenadi, heard about this regicide that happened in Magadha, and he thought, "That's terrible.
This is not a good king.
So I'm going to take back this particular province that I had given to King Bimbisara some time ago as a gift because he was such a just king.
I'm going to take that province back," a very wealthy province.
Ajatisattu, of course, was outraged that this province was being taken from his kingdom.
He attacked Pasenadi of Kosala, and there was a big war between Magadha and Kosala.
It was really a bad war and lots of people got killed.
At first it looked like Magadha was winning, and then it looked like Kosala was winning.
**Zoketsu Norman Fischer:** Back and forth, back and forth.
When Kosala won, Ajatisattu was defeated and captured, so King Pasenadi went to the Buddha and said, "What should I do?"
They were, as all the royals were in those days, and even today, all related.
"What am I going to do?
He's my cousin, he might be my nephew.
I don't want to hurt my nephew, but yet he's a prisoner of war.
What am I going to do with him?"
And the Buddha said, "Be merciful."
So Pasenadi said, "Okay, well, I'm going to release you from prison and you can go home and resume the throne.

But to make sure that we continue with good relations and there's no bad feelings, I'm going to offer you," and this was always done in those days among royalty, "I'm going to offer you the hand of my daughter in marriage so that we'll have connections, and I'm going to give you that province for a wedding present."
Ajatisattu was amazed by this, who wouldn't be?
It's like what happened at the end of World War II, with the United States and the European powers that opposed the United States.
The United States did the same thing, and it worked pretty well for everybody.
It worked really well here, except it didn't work so well for Devadatta.
When Ajatisattu reflected on the advice that had got him into this bad place, he realized that Devadatta's advice, which was supposed to be so great, didn't really help him.
So little by little he withdrew royal patronage from Devadatta, and little by little Devadatta was losing many disciples.
Many disciples came back.
There was one episode where some of the Buddha's disciples, I think maybe it was Shariputra, and some others just went to Devadatta's group.
Devadatta said, "Oh good, even Shariputra is coming over to my side."
They practiced there together with everybody, honoring Devadatta's teaching and honoring the sangha, for maybe two or three months, and then left without saying anything.
Many hundreds of monastics left with them.
So little by little Devadatta had fewer and fewer disciples, and finally no royal patronage, and he got seriously ill.
Time went by, and Ajatisattu was fine now.
He was in his kingdom, everything was peaceful, but he began feeling really badly.
He was tortured, really tortured, because without a war to fight and without anybody to oppose, he was just left with his own heart, and he began to feel the remorse for what he had done.
It was really terrible, what he did, and he began to feel every bit of it.
He was very upset.
So eventually he comes to the Buddha and asks the Buddha for help.
He was no longer studying with Devadatta, but up to now he had not been with the Buddha either.
Now he comes to the Buddha and says, "Can you help me?
I'm really tortured."
And the Buddha said, "Well, I'm going to speak to you and everybody here about the fruits of practice."
This is a famous teaching of the Buddha, the fruits of the holy life.
Some of this he was speaking to monastics, and he was talking about monastic life, but I think we can understand these fruits in our own lives.
He says the first advantage of practice is this.
We've all been hurt, we've all been abused, we've all been diminished, and maybe we don't have such a good feeling about our own lives.
When you have the discipline to practice, when you sit, when you are a member of a sangha, you have self-respect.

You really see that you can't but respect yourself, not because you're great or something special, but because you are doing something that you know is honorable, and like everybody else, you're deserving of self-respect.
That's the first fruit of the practice: your human dignity is restored.

The second fruit of the practice is that when you practice precepts, when you take care of your conduct and your behavior, taking care of yourself and taking care of others, pain in your life is reduced.
You're more relaxed, more at ease when you know you're following the path of justice and moral conduct.
The third fruit of the path is that when you practice you can't help but confront all of your fears, and when you confront your fears you're no longer plagued by them.
You're no longer scared of them.
You can be not afraid anymore of your own fear, and in that sense you can be fearless.

And then he said, "You know, your majesty, if you would practice breathing, if you would practice full awareness of breathing and meditation, you could experience the happiness of one who follows the path.
Meditation brings this kind of happiness.
Your majesty, if you dwell diligently in mindfulness, observing the precepts, you can really see into your own mind.
You can see the impermanent nature.
You can see there's nothing to grasp, as much as we grasp, that there's nothing to grasp.
And when you see that, you no longer have to be entangled by the inner tangle."
So you may still have the same problems.
Actually, because of what Ajatisattu did, he will never stop feeling remorse, but he doesn't have to be entangled and tortured by that remorse.
He can be disentangled from that tangle and find some peace.
And he said, "When you disentangle the tangle, it becomes clear to you that you practice for others and you can benefit others.
Benefiting others really brings you a lot of happiness."
So those are the fruits of the spiritual path.
Of course Ajatisattu was so moved by all this, and he said, "You have helped me see the true value of the dharma.
You have rebuilt in me that which was in ruins.
You have revealed that in me which was concealed.
You have shown a path to one who has been lost, and you brought light into the darkness.
Please accept me as a disciple and I will practice."
And the Buddha said, "Of course I will."
So this is a wonderful story of forgiveness and repentance.
When you think about this story, it tells you the power of mercy.
We would all have agreed if Ajatisattu were clapped in jail for the rest of his life.
We would all have agreed that he deserved it, and it would be a just dessert for him.
But instead he was given tremendous mercy.
And that mercy, I think, mattered.

If he had been clapped in jail, he would have been continuing on and on with his bitterness, and if he had had anybody who could have gotten him out of jail, he would have gotten out of jail and been a nefarious character in the area.
But because he was given a chance to just receive mercy, even though he didn't deserve it, he was then able to turn toward his own heart, and the remorse and pain of his own heart.
I think every heart, even of the most hardened, rotten person, left to their own devices under the influence of mercy, that person will see through bitter experience the need for repentance.
And repenting, going somewhere, and finding a way to commit oneself, as Ajatisattu does here, to a different life makes everything possible.
So it's something to think about, in all these cases in our own lives where repentance and forgiveness is needed.
